r3-p08-002: In stage 1, an ADXL355Z–DHT22–Raspberry Pi acquisition setup was built on a foam-board model about 55 cm long to verify the concept of temperature/humidity-compensated anomaly detection. Because damping and assembly variation in the foam board made the resonance peaks broad, stage 2 extended the same sensing and compensation setup to an aluminum multi-span model.

r3-p08-011: How temperature compensation behaves over seasonal change when a frequency-decision channel is combined with the autoencoder was checked with the openLAB dataset published by TU Dresden [8]. The structure is a three-span concrete research bridge about 45 m long; 526 records of air temperature, humidity and acceleration from spring to autumn 2024 are provided, and because the bridge was undamaged throughout, every alarm is a false alarm. In each
r3-p09-000: record, all three natural frequencies rose as the temperature fell (about −0.19%/°C for the 7.05 Hz mode), and the rise steepened below 15 °C, reaching 6–8% in October. The normal baseline and threshold were set from summer (May–June) records and applied unchanged to 69 autumn records (mid-September to October) to compare false-alarm rates by compensation method. The decision combined the current 8-feature autoencoder with a frequency channel that checks whether the compensated frequency of the 7.05 Hz mode — the mode most affected by temperature — falls outside the central 99% range of the summer records (0.5% excluded at each end); an alarm was counted if either channel was exceeded. Both channels use 99% of normal records as their reference.
r3-p09-010: [Figure 4: False-alarm rates by compensation method on 69 openLAB records from Sep–Oct with the frequency channel combined (summer baseline applied unchanged)]
r3-p09-011: With the original autoencoder alone, the anomaly score stayed at about 0.1× the threshold in October even though the frequency had risen by 6–8%, so it did not see the seasonal change at all. With the frequency channel combined and no compensation, 26% of the autumn records were judged anomalous, reproducing the surge in uncompensated false alarms reported in prior work [2] (Figure 4). Compensation with a first-order polynomial in air temperature lowered the false-alarm rate only to 17%, because a linear relationship learned over the summer cannot extrapolate the nonlinear rise at low temperatures. With second-order polynomial compensation the rate fell to 3%, and with second-order compensation on surface temperature to 0%, back to the level of the training period (about 2%). Relative humidity left the rate unchanged when added to the second-order air-temperature model (3→3%) and was therefore excluded, consistent with prior findings [2] that natural-frequency variation is explained mainly by temperature.
r3-p09-013: The tests have three purposes. First, to examine with low-cost sensors (2.2) and model bridges how changes in structural condition affect the vibration features and anomaly scores. Second, to verify the reduction in false alarms from temperature/humidity compensation; the full-scale comparison is handled by openLAB (2.7). Third, to move the validated system to two real pedestrian overpasses and examine environmental effects on bridge E and detection power on bridge C (stage 3). The core proof of performance is stage 2, where conditions can be controlled; stage 3 is supplementary validation in the field, where no damage labels exist.
